claims.hypothesis: Reactions of UV-pumped H2(v >= 2) molecules with S+ ions can explain the observed SH+ emission at the edge of the Orion Bar PDR without invoking elemental sulfur depletion.
claims.experiment: Imaged SH+ N_J = 1_0 - 0_1 at 1'' resolution with ALMA and modeled excitation and PDR chemistry including state-specific S+ + H2(v >= 2) rates in an isobaric Meudon PDR model coupled to a nonlocal Monte Carlo radiative transfer code.
claims.result: SH+ emission is confined to a ~10'' filament at A_V < 2 mag with N(SH+) ≃ 1.1x10^13 cm^-2, reproduced by models with P_th/k ≃ (1-2)x10^8 cm^-3 K and solar sulfur abundance (S/H = 1.4x10^-5).
claims.finding: UV-pumped H2(v >= 2) reactions with S+ explain the SH+ column density and spatial distribution in a high-pressure PDR surface layer with no or very little sulfur depletion.

evidence.loc: abstract
evidence.quote: We find that reactions of UV-pumped H 2 ( v ≥ 2) molecules with S [+] ions explain the presence of SH [+] in a high thermal-pressure gas component, P th / k ≈ 10 [8] cm [−][3] K, close to the H 2 dissociation front (at A V < 2 mag ).

evidence.loc: 6.3. Gas-grain PDR model results
evidence.quote: The resulting SH [+] abundance profile is nearly identical and there is no need to invoke depletion of elemental sulfur from the gas-phase to explain the observed SH [+] emission (see Fig. 15).

claims.hypothesis: Subsequent gas-phase hydrogen abstraction reactions of SH+, H2S+, and S with vibrationally excited H2(v >= 2) can form enough H2S+, H3S+, and SH to explain the observed H2S abundance in the Orion Bar.
claims.experiment: Performed ab initio quantum and QCT calculations for SH+ + H2(v) <-> H2S+ + H and S + H2(v) <-> SH + H, incorporated the new rates into pure gas-phase PDR models, and compared predicted column densities and line intensities with IRAM 30m and Herschel observations.
claims.result: SH+ is destroyed much faster by H atoms and electrons than it reacts with H2(v >= 2), S + H2(v >= 2) has a reaction barrier and slow rate, and pure gas-phase PDR models underestimate the observed N(H2S) = 2.5x10^14 cm^-2 by more than two orders of magnitude (log N = 10.6-11.7 vs ~14.4).
claims.finding: Gas-phase reactions with vibrationally excited H2 fail to overcome the bottlenecks to form H2S, missing the main H2S formation route.

evidence.loc: abstract
evidence.quote: However, subsequent hydrogen abstraction reactions of SH [+], H 2 S [+], and S atoms with vibrationally excited H 2, fail to form enough H 2 S [+], H 3 S [+], and SH to ultimately explain the observed H 2 S column density

evidence.loc: 7. Summary and conclusions
evidence.quote: In particular, pure gas-phase models underestimate the H 2 S column density observed in the Orion Bar by more than two orders of magnitude. This implies that these models miss the main H 2 S formation route.

claims.hypothesis: Freeze-out of S atoms with higher binding energies (E_b/k ~ 2600 K), grain surface hydrogenation to s-H2S, and subsequent photodesorption can explain the observed gas-phase H2S column density in the Orion Bar and other FUV-illuminated clouds.
claims.experiment: Built gas-grain PDR models comparing low and high adsorption binding energies for S and SH, including s-H2S surface formation, photodesorption, and chemical desorption, and ran models across a range of G0 and n_H.
claims.result: The high E_b gas-grain model yields log N(H2S) = 13.7-14.8 cm^-2, matching the observed ~14.4 and line intensities, and predicts a nearly constant H2S column density (a few 10^14 cm^-2) and peak abundance (a few 10^-8) almost independent of n_H and G0.
claims.finding: Grain surface formation of s-H2S at T_d < 50 K (enabled by higher S and SH binding energies) followed by photodesorption explains the observed H2S abundances in the Orion Bar and dark cloud edges without requiring large elemental sulfur depletion.

evidence.loc: abstract
evidence.quote: Photodesorption and, to a lesser extent, chemical desorption, produce roughly the same H 2 S column density (a few 10 [14] cm [−][2] ) and abundance peak (a few 10 [−][8] ) nearly independently of n H and G 0 .

evidence.loc: 7. Summary and conclusions
evidence.quote: Indeed, the observed N (H 2 S) in the Orion Bar can only be explained by the freeze-out of S atoms, grain surface formation of s-H 2 S mantles, and subsequent photodesorption back to the gas phase.

why_this_data.value: The Orion Bar is seen nearly edge-on, allowing spatial resolution of the ionization and dissociation fronts and chemical stratification; ALMA 1'' imaging resolves the narrow SH+ filament, while SOFIA/GREAT accesses the 1383 GHz SH ground-state rotational lines that lie in a frequency gap inaccessible to Herschel/HIFI.

why_this_method.value: Reactive molecular ions like SH+ have short lifetimes comparable to nonreactive collision timescales, requiring chemical formation and destruction rates in the statistical equilibrium equations within a nonlocal Monte Carlo radiative transfer code; state-specific ab initio quantum rates are required because FUV-pumped H2(v >= 1) drives endoergic reactions out of thermal equilibrium.

referee_caveats_inferred: Single-dish observations of H2S (IRAM 30m, 15''-8'' beam; Herschel/HIFI, 42''-20'' beam) and SH (SOFIA, 20'' beam) have much coarser angular resolution than the 1'' ALMA SH+ image, introducing beam-dilution and spatial-coincidence uncertainties when jointly modeling the DF.

Surface hydrogenation reactions on grains are treated as instantaneous whenever H-atom sticking timescales are shorter than desorption timescales, rather than solving a full rate-equation or microscopic Monte Carlo grain-surface network.
